## Claude — 2026-11-18T17:20:41.284Z

They **can** be compile-time generated, but **MSVC rejects constexpr C-arrays initialized by lambdas**:

```cpp
// This FAILS on MSVC:
constexpr int PEERS[81][20] = []() {
    int peers[81][20] = {};
    // fill...
    return peers;
}();
```

**Error:** `error C2440: 'initializing': cannot convert from 'int (*)[20]' to 'const int [81][20]'`

MSVC's constexpr support for C-arrays with lambda initializers is broken — it treats the lambda return type as a pointer (`int(*)[20]`) rather than the array type (`int[81][20]`).

## Workarounds That Work

| Approach | MSVC | GCC/Clang |
|----------|------|-----------|
| `constexpr std::array<...> = [](){...}();` | ❌ | ✅ |
| `constexpr int arr[N] = [](){...}();` | ❌ | ✅ |
| `constexpr int arr[N][M] = [](){...}();` | ❌ | ❌ |
| `static int arr[N][M];` + runtime init | ✅ | ✅ |

## Why Not Template Metaprogramming?

Could use recursive templates, but:
- **Verbose** — 100+ lines of template metaprogramming
- **Slow compile times** — deep template instantiation
- **Hard to maintain** — obscure syntax

## The Pragmatic Choice

Runtime initialization via global static constructor:
```cpp
int Sudoku::PEERS[81][20];
int Sudoku::BOX_CELLS[9][9];

struct Init { Init() { /* fill arrays */ } } g_init;
```

- **One-time cost** at program startup (~microseconds)
- **Zero runtime overhead** after init (arrays in `.data`, direct access)
- **Works everywhere** — MSVC, GCC, Clang, ICC
- **Simple, readable, maintainable**

For 9×9 Sudoku tables (3240 ints total), the startup cost is negligible. The `constexpr` benefit (zero-init in `.rodata` vs runtime init in `.data`) doesn't matter for hot-path performance — both are cache-friendly after first access.

There is, however, a way to achieve exactly what you want: generate the tables at compile time while retaining C-style arrays.
1. Why the original approach fails
Consider:
constexpr int PEERS[81][20] = []() {
    int peers[81][20] = {};

    // Fill peers...

    return peers;
}();


The problem is that C-style arrays cannot be returned by value from a C++ function or lambda.

When you write:
return peers;


the array undergoes array-to-pointer decay. The resulting return type is effectively:
int (*)[20]


That is a pointer to an array of 20 integers, not an array of 81 × 20 integers.

Consequently, MSVC is correct to reject the initialization.

This is also invalid in standard C++:
constexpr int arr[10] = []() {
    int values[10] = {};
    return values;
}();


GCC and Clang should reject this too. The compatibility table in your text is misleading.
2. Solution: Use a struct containing C-style arrays
You can actually return a structure containing C-style arrays by value.

This gives you compile-time initialization without having to switch to std::array.
struct SudokuTables
{
    int PEERS[81][20];
    int BOX_CELLS[9][9];
};

constexpr SudokuTables GenerateTables()
{
    SudokuTables tables{};

    // Generate PEERS.
    for (int cell = 0; cell < 81; ++cell)
    {
        const int row = cell / 9;
        const int col = cell % 9;
        const int box = (row / 3) * 3 + col / 3;

        int count = 0;

        for (int other = 0; other < 81; ++other)
        {
            if (other == cell)
                continue;

            const int otherRow = other / 9;
            const int otherCol = other % 9;
            const int otherBox = (otherRow / 3) * 3 + otherCol / 3;

            if (otherRow == row ||
                otherCol == col ||
                otherBox == box)
            {
                tables.PEERS[cell][count++] = other;
            }
        }
    }

    // Generate BOX_CELLS.
    for (int box = 0; box < 9; ++box)
    {
        int count = 0;

        for (int cell = 0; cell < 81; ++cell)
        {
            const int row = cell / 9;
            const int col = cell % 9;

            if ((row / 3) * 3 + col / 3 == box)
                tables.BOX_CELLS[box][count++] = cell;
        }
    }

    return tables;
}

// Compile-time initialization.
inline constexpr SudokuTables TABLES = GenerateTables();

// Convenient C-style array access.
inline constexpr auto& PEERS = TABLES.PEERS;
inline constexpr auto& BOX_CELLS = TABLES.BOX_CELLS;


This works with C++17, including MSVC implementations supporting the required constexpr functionality.

You can still access the arrays exactly as before:
int peer = PEERS[cell][i];
int boxCell = BOX_CELLS[box][i];


The arrays are compile-time initialized and immutable.
3. Why this approach is interesting
Property	Runtime initialization	Struct + constexpr
Compile-time generation	No	Yes
C-style arrays	Yes	Yes
Runtime initialization cost	Yes	No
Immutable data	Not necessarily	Yes
Direct array indexing	Yes	Yes
MSVC support	Yes	Yes, with C++17 support

The compiler can put the resulting constant data into read-only storage, depending on the target and compiler implementation.

There is no need for a global initialization constructor.
4. My recommendation
For your Sudoku solver, I would use the struct-based approach.

There is no reason to sacrifice compile-time generation simply because you want to retain C-style arrays.

One additional consideration: if these declarations are in a header, inline constexpr (C++17) avoids multiple-definition problems while allowing the tables to be shared across translation units.

The important distinction: C++ cannot return a C-style array directly, but it can return an object containing C-style arrays. That distinction makes this solution possible.
</pasted_content id="da2c">

642	// Bit-packed grid utilities
643	Sudoku::PackedGrid Sudoku::packGrid(const Grid& grid)
644	{
645		PackedGrid packed = {};
646		for (int i = 0; i < 81; ++i) {
647			int bit_pos = i * 4;
648			int word = bit_pos / 64;
649			int shift = bit_pos % 64;
650			packed[word] |= (static_cast<uint64_t>(grid[i]) << shift);
651		}
652		return packed;
653	}
654	
655	Sudoku::Grid Sudoku::unpackGrid(const PackedGrid& packed)
656	{
657		Grid grid = {};
658		for (int i = 0; i < 81; ++i) {
659			int bit_pos = i * 4;
660			int word = bit_pos / 64;
661			int shift = bit_pos % 64;
662			grid[i] = static_cast<uint16_t>((packed[word] >> shift) & 0xF);
663		}
664		return grid;
665	}

## Claude — 2026-11-18T17:27:03.486Z

Done. The `constexpr struct` approach works perfectly:

```cpp
// Outside class - compile-time generation
struct SudokuTables { int PEERS[81][20]; int BOX_CELLS[9][9]; };

constexpr SudokuTables GenerateTables() { /* fill via loops */ return tables; }

inline constexpr SudokuTables TABLES = GenerateTables();

// Const references to C-arrays (no runtime cost)
inline constexpr const int (&PEERS)[81][20] = TABLES.PEERS;
inline constexpr const int (&BOX_CELLS)[9][9] = TABLES.BOX_CELLS;
```

**Why this works:**
- Structs **can** be returned by value from constexpr functions
- C-arrays inside structs are preserved (no decay)
- `TABLES` is `constexpr` → data in `.rodata` (read-only section)
- References are `constexpr` → zero overhead, direct access
- Works on MSVC/GCC/Clang with C++17

**Benchmarks unchanged:** Bitmask 1.63 µs avg (example), 11.06 µs avg (hard) — still faster than DLX.

## Claude — 2026-11-18T17:29:12.313Z

`std::array` is **fine for `Grid`** — it's not preventing anything here.

## Why `std::array` Works for `Grid`

```cpp
static constexpr Grid EXAMPLE_PUZZLE = {
    5,3,0, 0,7,0, 0,0,0,
    6,0,0, 1,9,5, 0,0,0,
    // ...
};
```

This works because:
- **Brace initialization** — literal values, no computation needed
- **Aggregate initialization** — `std::array` is an aggregate since C++17
- **No lambda required** — values are written directly

## The Difference

| Case | Initialization | Works with `std::array`? |
|------|----------------|--------------------------|
| `EXAMPLE_PUZZLE` | Literal braces `{5,3,0,...}` | ✅ Yes |
| `PEERS[81][20]` | Computed via loops | ❌ No (lambda returns decayed pointer) |

## When You Need the Struct Trick

Only when **generating values algorithmically at compile time**:
```cpp
// This FAILS for std::array (same C-array decay issue)
constexpr std::array<std::array<int,20>,81> PEERS = []() {
    std::array<std::array<int,20>,81> p{};
    for (...) p[i][j] = ...;
    return p;  // C++17: std::array CAN be returned by value!
}();

// Wait — std::array CAN be returned by value!
```

**Actually — `std::array` CAN be returned by value from lambdas!** The decay problem is **C-arrays only**.

## So We Could Use `std::array` for PEERS/BOX_CELLS Too

```cpp
constexpr std::array<std::array<int,20>,81> GeneratePeers() { ... }
inline constexpr auto PEERS = GeneratePeers();  // Works!
```

The struct trick was only needed because we wanted **C-arrays** for zero-overhead direct indexing. With `std::array`, no trick needed — but you get `.size()`, iterators, bounds checking.

**Verdict:** Keep `std::array` for `Grid`. It's the right tool for puzzle data. The struct workaround was only for the computed lookup tables where we wanted C-array performance.

## Claude — 2026-11-18T17:30:42.094Z

**Yes, `std::array` would be simpler and better** — it works directly with `constexpr` lambdas (no struct workaround needed):

```cpp
// This WORKS for std::array (C++17)
constexpr std::array<std::array<int, 20>, 81> GeneratePeers() {
    std::array<std::array<int, 20>, 81> p{};
    for (int i = 0; i < 81; ++i) {
        // fill p[i]...
    }
    return p;  // ✅ std::array CAN be returned by value!
}

inline constexpr auto PEERS = GeneratePeers();  // Works!
```

## Comparison

| Feature | C-array (current) | `std::array` |
|---------|-------------------|--------------|
| Compile-time generation | Needs struct trick | Direct lambda |
| Indexing syntax | `PEERS[cell][k]` | `PEERS[cell][k]` (same!) |
| Bounds checking | ❌ | Optional via `.at()` |
| `.size()` | ❌ | ✅ |
| Range-for / structured bindings | ❌ | ✅ |
| Performance | Zero overhead | Zero overhead |

## Simpler Code

```cpp
// Replace the struct trick with:
inline constexpr auto PEERS = []() {
    std::array<std::array<int, 20>, 81> p{};
    // fill...
    return p;
}();

inline constexpr auto BOX_CELLS = []() {
    std::array<std::array<int, 9>, 9> b{};
    // fill...
    return b;
}();
```

**Verdict:** Switch to `std::array` — simpler, more idiomatic, same performance, and avoids the struct workaround entirely. Want me to make the change?

## Claude — 2026-11-18T17:39:23.704Z

Done. The lookup tables are now encapsulated inside the `Sudoku` class:

```cpp
class Sudoku {
public:
    // ...
    
    // Compile-time generated lookup tables (inline lambdas, C++17)
    static constexpr auto PEERS = []() {
        std::array<std::array<int, 20>, 81> p{};
        // fill...
        return p;
    }();

    static constexpr auto BOX_CELLS = []() {
        std::array<std::array<int, 9>, 9> b{};
        // fill...
        return b;
    }();
};
```

**Benefits:**
- ✅ Encapsulated within `Sudoku` (accessed as `Sudoku::PEERS`)
- ✅ Compile-time generation via inline lambdas
- ✅ Zero runtime overhead
- ✅ Clean, self-contained class definition
- ✅ Performance unchanged (1.6 µs avg)

14	## Key Design Decisions
15	
16	1. **Member variables early** — declared in `private:` section before public interface for visible memory layout
17	2. **Leading underscore** — `_grid`, `_solution`, `_solved` for private members

<pasted_content id="da2c">
Critical Issues Found
State corruption when backtracking in Sudoku::_solveRecursive() (src/Sudoku.cpp:544-592)

_solveRecursive() calls _propagate() after placing a candidate, which modifies _solution, _rows, _cols, _boxes, and _cell_candidates across the whole board.
On backtrack (lines 579-589), only cell and its 20 PEERS candidate masks (saved[20]) are restored. Any cells filled or candidates eliminated by _propagate() during the failed branch are never undone, leaving the board corrupted for subsequent candidate branches.
Additionally, _propagate() (lines 361-370) always returns true and does not detect contradictions, and _cell_candidates[cell] is not saved/restored if _updateCandidates() clears it during propagation.
30-byte out-of-bounds read in AVX2 _findBestCell() and _nakedSingles() (src/Sudoku.cpp:290-292, 387-389)

When base == 80, process == 1, but _mm256_loadu_si256 unconditionally reads 32 bytes (16 × uint16_t) starting at &_cell_candidates[80] and &_solution[80].
Since _cell_candidates[81] is the last member of Sudoku, this reads 30 bytes past the end of the Sudoku object (undefined behavior / potential access violation near a page boundary). Masking vec_cand afterward does not prevent the load. Padding _solution and _cell_candidates (e.g., to 96 elements) or handling process < 16 via scalar code avoids the over-read.
Missing root sentinel in SudokuDLX::search() causes infinite loop (src/SudokuDLX.cpp:150-169)

headers[0] (cellCol(0, 0)) is both a real constraint column and the sentinel for the circular header list (headers[0]->right == headers[0] and c != headers[0]).
Because the search loop starts at headers[0]->right, headers[0] is never selected directly as best_col. On the current 3 test puzzles, (0, 0) happens to stay uncovered until the end.
Whenever (0, 0) is covered while other columns remain (e.g., puzzles requiring deeper branching or conflicting givens), cover(headers[0]) unlinks headers[0] from the ring while leaving headers[0]->right pointing to another node. Subsequent calls to search() either traverse a ring that no longer contains headers[0] (infinite loop once no column has size <= 1) or fail to reach the headers[0]->right == headers[0] base case. Adding a dedicated dummy root header node fixes this.
</pasted_content id="da2c">

69	void SudokuDLX::buildMatrix(const Grid& puzzle, Node* headers[COLS])
70	{
71		// For each possible placement (r, c, d)
72		for (int r = 0; r < 9; ++r)
73		{
74			for (int c = 0; c < 9; ++c)
75			{
76				for (int d = 1; d <= 9; ++d)
77				{
78					// If puzzle has a given, only allow that digit
79					if (puzzle[idx(r, c)] != 0 && puzzle[idx(r, c)] != d)
80						continue;
81	
82					int row_id = r * 81 + c * 9 + (d - 1);
83					int b = boxOf(r, c);
84	
85					// Four constraints for this placement
86					int cols[4] = {
87						cellCol(r, c),      // cell (r,c) filled
88						rowCol(r, d),       // row r has digit d
89						colCol(c, d),       // col c has digit d
90						boxCol(b, d)        // box b has digit d
91					};
92	
93					Node* first = nullptr;
94					Node* prev = nullptr;
95	
96					for (int ci = 0; ci < 4; ++ci)
97					{
98						int col_idx = cols[ci];
99						Node* node = &g_node_buffer[g_node_count++];
100						node->row_id = row_id;
101						node->constraint_id = col_idx;
102						node->column = headers[col_idx];
103	
104						// Link vertically (at bottom of column)
105						node->up = headers[col_idx]->up;
106						node->down = headers[col_idx];
107						headers[col_idx]->up->down = node;
108						headers[col_idx]->up = node;
109						headers[col_idx]->size++;

117						}
118						else

121							node->right = first;
122							prev->right = node;

125						}
126					}
127				}
128			}
129		}
130	}
131	
132	void SudokuDLX::cover(Node* c)
133	{
134		// Remove column header from horizontal list
135		c->right->left = c->left;
136		c->left->right = c->right;
137	
138		// Remove all rows in this column from other columns
139		for (Node* i = c->down; i != c; i = i->down)
140		{
141			for (Node* j = i->right; j != i; j = j->right)
142			{
143				j->down->up = j->up;
144				j->up->down = j->down;
145				j->column->size--;
146			}
147		}
148	}
149	
150	void SudokuDLX::uncover(Node* c)
151	{
152		// Restore rows in reverse order
153		for (Node* i = c->up; i != c; i = i->up)
154		{
155			for (Node* j = i->left; j != i; j = j->left)
156			{
157				j->column->size++;
158				j->down->up = j;
159				j->up->down = j;
160			}
161		}
162	
163		// Restore column header to horizontal list
164		c->right->left = c;
165		c->left->right = c;
166	}
167	
168	bool SudokuDLX::search(Node* headers[COLS], int* solution_rows, int& solution_count, int depth)
169	{
170		// If header points to itself, all columns covered = solved
171		if (headers[0]->right == headers[0])
172		{
173			return true;
174		}
175	
176		// Choose column with minimum size (Knuth's S heuristic)
177		Node* best_col = nullptr;
178		int min_size = INT_MAX;
179	
180		for (Node* c = headers[0]->right; c != headers[0]; c = c->right)
181		{
182			if (c->size < min_size)
183			{
184				min_size = c->size;
185				best_col = c;
186	
187				if (min_size == 0)
188					return false; // dead end
189	
190				if (min_size == 1)
191					break; // optimal
192			}
193		}
194	
195		if (!best_col || min_size == 0)
196			return false;
197	
198		cover(best_col);
199	
200		// Try each row in this column
201		for (Node* r = best_col->down; r != best_col; r = r->down)
202		{
203			solution_rows[solution_count++] = r->row_id;
204	
205			// Cover all other columns in this row
206			for (Node* j = r->right; j != r; j = j->right)
207			{
208				cover(j->column);
209			}
210	
211			if (search(headers, solution_rows, solution_count, depth + 1))
212				return true;
213	
214			// Backtrack
215			--solution_count;
216			for (Node* j = r->left; j != r; j = j->left)
217			{
218				uncover(j->column);
219			}
220		}
221	
222		uncover(best_col);
223		return false;
224	}

  "old_string": "bool SudokuDLX::search(Node* headers[COLS], int* solution_rows, int& solution_count, int depth)\n{\n\t// If header points to itself, all columns covered = solved\n\tif (headers[0]->right == headers[0])\n\t{\n\t\treturn true;\n\t}\n\n\t// Choose column with minimum size (Knuth's S heuristic)\n\tNode* best_col = nullptr;\n\tint min_size = INT_MAX;\n\n\tfor (Node* c = headers[0]->right; c != headers[0]; c = c->right)\n\t{\n\t\tif (c->size < min_size)\n\t\t{\n\t\t\tmin_size = c->size;\n\t\t\tbest_col = c;\n\n\t\t\tif (min_size == 0)\n\t\t\t\treturn false; // dead end\n\n\t\t\tif (min_size == 1)\n\t\t\t\tbreak; // optimal\n\t\t}\n\t}\n\n\tif (!best_col || min_size == 0)\n\t\treturn false;\n\n\tcover(best_col);\n\n\t// Try each row in this column\n\tfor (Node* r = best_col->down; r != best_col; r = r->down)\n\t{\n\t\tsolution_rows[solution_count++] = r->row_id;\n\n\t\t// Cover all other columns in this row\n\t\tfor (Node* j = r->right; j != r; j = j->right)\n\t\t{\n\t\t\tcover(j->column);\n\t\t}\n\n\t\tif (search(headers, solution_rows, solution_count, depth + 1))\n\t\t\treturn true;\n\n\t\t// Backtrack\n\t\t--solution_count;\n\t\tfor (Node* j = r->left; j != r; j = j->left)\n\t\t{\n\t\t\tuncover(j->column);\n\t\t}\n\t}\n\n\tuncover(best_col);\n\treturn false;\n}",
  "new_string": "bool SudokuDLX::search(Node* root, int* solution_rows, int& solution_count, int depth)\n{\n\t// If root points to itself, all columns covered = solved\n\tif (root->right == root)\n\t{\n\t\treturn true;\n\t}\n\n\t// Choose column with minimum size (Knuth's S heuristic)\n\tNode* best_col = nullptr;\n\tint min_size = INT_MAX;\n\n\tfor (Node* c = root->right; c != root; c = c->right)\n\t{\n\t\tif (c->size < min_size)\n\t\t{\n\t\t\tmin_size = c->size;\n\t\t\tbest_col = c;\n\n\t\t\tif (min_size == 0)\n\t\t\t\treturn false; // dead end\n\n\t\t\tif (min_size == 1)\n\t\t\t\tbreak; // optimal\n\t\t}\n\t}\n\n\tif (!best_col || min_size == 0)\n\t\treturn false;\n\n\tcover(best_col);\n\n\t// Try each row in this column\n\tfor (Node* r = best_col->down; r != best_col; r = r->down)\n\t{\n\t\tsolution_rows[solution_count++] = r->row_id;\n\n\t\t// Cover all other columns in this row\n\t\tfor (Node* j = r->right; j != r; j = j->right)\n\t\t{\n\t\t\tcover(j->column);\n\t\t}\n\n\t\tif (search(root, solution_rows, solution_count, depth + 1))\n\t\t\treturn true;\n\n\t\t// Backtrack\n\t\t--solution_count;\n\t\tfor (Node* j = r->left; j != r; j = j->left)\n\t\t{\n\t\t\tuncover(j->column);\n\t\t}\n\t}\n\n\tuncover(best_col);\n\treturn false;\n}"

591	bool Sudoku::_solveRecursive()
592	{
593		int cell = _findBestCell();
594		if (cell == -1) {
595			// No cell with candidates found - check if solved or contradiction
596			for (int i = 0; i < 81; ++i) {

608		while (candidates) {
609			Mask m = candidates & -candidates;

614			_solution[cell] = num;

623	
624			for (int i = 0; i < 81; ++i) {

626				saved_solution[i] = _solution[i];
627			}

642			// Apply constraint propagation after placement
643			if (_propagate()) {

663	// Bit-packed grid utilities
664	Sudoku::PackedGrid Sudoku::packGrid(const Grid& grid)
665	{
666		PackedGrid packed = {};
667		for (int i = 0; i < 81; ++i) {
668			int bit_pos = i * 4;
669			int word = bit_pos / 64;
670			int shift = bit_pos % 64;
671			packed[word] |= (static_cast<uint64_t>(grid[i]) << shift);
672		}
673		return packed;
674	}
675	
676	Sudoku::Grid Sudoku::unpackGrid(const PackedGrid& packed)
677	{
678		Grid grid = {};
679		for (int i = 0; i < 81; ++i) {
680			int bit_pos = i * 4;
681			int word = bit_pos / 64;
682			int shift = bit_pos % 64;
683			grid[i] = static_cast<uint16_t>((packed[word] >> shift) & 0xF);
684		}
685		return grid;
686	}

Let me fix this by collecting all hidden singles first, then placing them all at once:



Now I understand the bug. The hidden singles are placed immediately, updating row/col/box masks, but candidate masks for intersecting houses remain stale. Let me fix this:

672	Sudoku::PackedGrid Sudoku::packGrid(const Grid& grid)
673	{
674		PackedGrid packed = {};
675		for (int i = 0; i < 81; ++i) {
676			int bit_pos = i * 4;

678			int shift = bit_pos % 64;
679			packed[word] |= (static_cast<uint64_t>(grid[i]) << shift);

2. Key Technical Concepts:

3. Files and Code Sections:

   - **src/Sudoku.cpp**: Implementation with AVX2 namespace, _findBestCell (AVX2 + scalar MRV), _nakedSingles (AVX2 vectorized), _hiddenSingles (collect-then-place), _propagate, _solveRecursive (depth-limited, full state save/restore), packGrid/unpackGrid

596	bool Sudoku::_solveRecursive(int depth)
597	{
598		// Safety: limit recursion depth to prevent stack overflow
599		if (depth > 81) return false;
600	
601		int cell = _findBestCell();
602		if (cell == -1) {
603			// No cell with candidates found - check if solved or contradiction
604			for (int i = 0; i < 81; ++i) {
605				if (_solution[i] == 0) return false; // empty cell with 0 candidates = contradiction
606			}
607			return true; // completely filled = solved
608		}
609	
610		Mask candidates = _cell_candidates[cell];
611		if (candidates == 0)
612			return false;
613	
614		int row = cell / 9;
615		int col = cell % 9;
616		int b = BOX_OF[cell];
617	
618		// Try each candidate (use member arrays to avoid stack overflow)
619		while (candidates) {
620			Mask m = candidates & -candidates;
621			int num = ctz(m);
622			candidates &= candidates - 1;
623	
624			// Place digit
625			_solution[cell] = num;
626			_rows[row] |= m;
627			_cols[col] |= m;
628			_boxes[b] |= m;
629	
630			// Save full state before propagation (propagation can modify many cells)
631			for (int i = 0; i < 81; ++i) {
632				_saved_candidates[i] = _cell_candidates[i];
633				_saved_solution[i] = _solution[i];
634			}
635			for (int i = 0; i < 9; ++i) {

637				_saved_cols[i] = _cols[i];
638				_saved_boxes[i] = _boxes[i];
639			}
640	
641			// Recompute ALL candidates from updated masks (not just peers)
642	// This ensures _propagate() works with fresh candidate data
643			for (int r = 0; r < N; ++r) {
644				for (int c = 0; c < N; ++c) {
645					_updateCandidates(r, c);
646				}
647			}
648	
649			// Apply constraint propagation after placement
650			if (_propagate()) {
651				if (_solveRecursive(depth + 1))
652					return true;
653			}
654	
655			// Backtrack - restore full state
656			for (int i = 0; i < 81; ++i) {

658				_solution[i] = _saved_solution[i];

670	// Bit-packed grid utilities
671	Sudoku::PackedGrid Sudoku::packGrid(const Grid& grid)
672	{
673		PackedGrid packed = {};
674		for (int i = 0; i < 81; ++i) {
675			int bit_pos = i * 4;
676			int word = bit_pos / 64;
677			int shift = bit_pos % 64;
678			packed[word] |= (static_cast<uint64_t>(grid[i]) << shift);
679		}
680		return packed;
681	}
682	
683	Sudoku::Grid Sudoku::unpackGrid(const PackedGrid& packed)
684	{
685		Grid grid = {};
686		for (int i = 0; i < 81; ++i) {
687			int bit_pos = i * 4;
688			int word = bit_pos / 64;
689			int shift = bit_pos % 64;
690			grid[i] = static_cast<uint16_t>((packed[word] >> shift) & 0xF);
691		}
692		return grid;
693	}

670	// Bit-packed grid utilities
671	Sudoku::PackedGrid Sudoku::packGrid(const Grid& grid)
672	{
673		PackedGrid packed = {};
674		for (int i = 0; i < 81; ++i) {
675			int bit_pos = i * 4;
676			int word = bit_pos / 64;
677			int shift = bit_pos % 64;
678			packed[word] |= (static_cast<uint64_t>(grid[i]) << shift);
679		}
680		return packed;
681	}
682	
683	Sudoku::Grid Sudoku::unpackGrid(const PackedGrid& packed)
684	{
685		Grid grid = {};
686		for (int i = 0; i < 81; ++i) {
687			int bit_pos = i * 4;
688			int word = bit_pos / 64;
689			int shift = bit_pos % 64;
690			grid[i] = static_cast<uint16_t>((packed[word] >> shift) & 0xF);
691		}
692		return grid;
693	}

674	// Bit-packed grid utilities
675	Sudoku::PackedGrid Sudoku::packGrid(const Grid& grid)
676	{
677		PackedGrid packed = {};
678		for (int i = 0; i < 81; ++i) {
679			int bit_pos = i * 4;
680			int word = bit_pos / 64;
681			int shift = bit_pos % 64;
682			packed[word] |= (static_cast<uint64_t>(grid[i]) << shift);
683		}
684		return packed;
685	}
686	
687	Sudoku::Grid Sudoku::unpackGrid(const PackedGrid& packed)
688	{
689		Grid grid = {};
690		for (int i = 0; i < 81; ++i) {
691			int bit_pos = i * 4;
692			int word = bit_pos / 64;
693			int shift = bit_pos % 64;
694			grid[i] = static_cast<uint16_t>((packed[word] >> shift) & 0xF);
695		}
696		return grid;
697	}

bool Sudoku::_hiddenSingles()
{
	bool progress = false;

	// Check rows
	for (int r = 0; r < N; ++r) {
		for (int d = 1; d <= 9; ++d) {
			Mask m = DIGIT_MASK[d];
			if (_rows[r] & m) continue;
			int count = 0, last_c = -1;
			for (int c = 0; c < N; ++c) {
				int i = idx(r, c);

					count++;
					last_c = c;
				}
			}
			if (count == 1) {
				int i = idx(r, last_c);
				_solution[i] = d;
				_rows[r] |= m;
				_cols[last_c] |= m;
				_boxes[BOX_OF[i]] |= m;
				_cell_candidates[i] = 0;
				progress = true;
			}
		}
	}

	// Check columns
	for (int c = 0; c < N; ++c) {
		for (int d = 1; d <= 9; ++d) {
			Mask m = DIGIT_MASK[d];
			if (_cols[c] & m) continue;
			int count = 0, last_r = -1;
			for (int r = 0; r < N; ++r) {
				int i = idx(r, c);
				if (_solution[i] == 0 && (_cell_candidates[i] & m)) {
					count++;
					last_r = r;
				}
			}
			if (count == 1) {
				int i = idx(last_r, c);
				_solution[i] = d;
				_rows[last_r] |= m;
				_cols[c] |= m;
				_boxes[BOX_OF[i]] |= m;
				_cell_candidates[i] = 0;
				progress = true;
			}
		}
	}

	// Check boxes - use precomputed BOX_CELLS for 9x speedup
	for (int b = 0; b < 9; ++b) {
		for (int d = 1; d <= 9; ++d) {
			Mask m = DIGIT_MASK[d];
			if (_boxes[b] & m) continue;
			int count = 0, last_cell = -1;
			// Iterate only 9 cells in this box instead of all 81

				_rows[r] |= m;

				_cell_candidates[last_cell] = 0;
				progress = true;
			}
		}
	}

		for (int r = 0; r < N; ++r) {
			for (int c = 0; c < N; ++c) {
				_updateCandidates(r, c);
			}
		}
	}
	return progress;
}

		int remaining = 81 - base;
